title: Jizo Bodhisattva
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk explores the concept of Bodhisattvas in Mahayana Buddhism, specifically focusing on Jizo, a Japanese Buddhist deity who embodies compassion and helps beings overcome negative karma. Through his teachings, Jizo emphasizes the importance of understanding and liberation, offering protection and blessings to travelers and those in need. By embracing our obligations and showing up with a sense of duty, we can cultivate a consistent practice and bring joy and delight to our spiritual journey.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
I really appreciate Chris's genius move to invite the bodhisattvas to be the guest speakers during practice period.

The impetus, she probably shared, is that she was feeling a little overwhelmed, and it's an extra layer of administration and effort to line up lots of guest speakers, which she has done so beautifully for the last couple of years.

He's a big music fan, which is wonderful.

I recommend it.

Our brains like that.
Whether it's essential, I don't know.

The Mahayana Buddhist movement seems to have emerged out of the early Buddhist schools, which had already divided into lots of different schools a couple of hundred years after the Buddha's likely dates.
They don't even exactly know which century the Buddha lived in.
It's plus or minus eighty-something years.

And we know from Chinese pilgrims who traveled through, a principal one being a favorite character of mine, a guy named Xuanzang in the 700s, that when he passed through the great monasteries of India and the kingdoms along the Silk Road, which also practiced Buddhism (it spread there, and then from there began to spread into China), it's not like there were some monasteries that were this later school, Mahayana, and some that were the earlier schools.
They were all kind of mixed together.
That sectarianism seems to be a more modern idea, as used to it as we are.

The Mahayana, which means great vehicle, seems to have emerged from within the ranks somewhere around the turning of the common era and just gradually swelled, and then he's there six, seven hundred years later.
But it's not at all like Catholicism and Protestantism.
There were no theses nailed to any doors.
It was more like a spread of ideas, and within the same exact place you had people more interested in one set of teachings and people more interested in the earlier set of teachings.

We tend now to call the earlier Buddhism either just early Buddhism, which is probably the simplest, or we use the term Theravada, which is a little confusing because Theravada is just one of the remaining early schools.
Back in the day, you wouldn't say Theravada as a global term.
It was just one of the early Buddhist schools, but they survived, so they get naming rights.
Sometimes you see people talking about this early Buddhism as Hinayana, but that's actually an insult.
It's a pejorative that this new movement, the Mahayana, used: Mahayana meaning great school and Hinayana meaning lesser school.
You still see that some, especially in the Tibetan Buddhist world, which seems a little weird to me.
If you ask them about it, they say, oh, we don't mean no disrespect, it's just what it's called.
But we usually will say Theravada or early Buddhism.
Early Buddhism is, in rough terms, more focused on individual practice, systematic practice.
Hey, there's Chris.
Hi.
And very precise, with the goal of complete peacefulness and depth as a practitioner.
Wonderful, wonderful.
It also includes what is emphasized in the Mahayana, but less so.

The Mahayana school emphasizes compassion more, and is more inclusive of lay practitioners, although it's still a pretty monastic movement. [unclear: "So I want to whitewash that and invented"] this great idea of the Bodhisattva.
In early Buddhism, the Bodhisattva only meant one thing.
It only meant the being who was about to become the Buddha of this current age, and you just get one at a time.

But luckily, since there's infinite time, and it's a cyclical worldview of time from India, there have been gazillions of Buddhas, just one at a time, going back a gazillion trillion, a billion years.
So the Mahayana folks said, no, no, no, no, no, there are a lot more Bodhisattvas than that.
We all can be Bodhisattvas.
We all are Bodhisattvas.
And some Bodhisattvas really went for it and went through intensive training, ten stages, and became these great Bodhisattvas.
So that's what we're looking at in this series: the great Bodhisattvas.
I'm coming in here after Manjushri, the Bodhisattva of wisdom, Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva of great activity, and Avalokiteshvara, the Bodhisattva of compassion.
This week we have Jizo, or Kshetigarbha, Bodhisattva of lots of things: children, travelers, support.
I was trying to distill it down in my mind to their principal expression, like facial expression.
I would say more or less Manjushri is pretty fierce.
This is tough love, grandpa and grandma.
So Manjushri is kind of stern.
And Manjushri in the traditional Zen hall would be the main statue.
Manjushri is all about wisdom, and the Zen school is all about wisdom, so you wouldn't normally have a Buddha figure in the Zendo.
You'd have Manjushri, Japanese Monju, the sacred monk.
Samantabhadra, I guess, is wide-eyed and excited, because Samantabhadra is the Bodhisattva of activity and going for it and just rolling along.
Chris's favorite, so I'm sure you had a great enthusiastic talk about Samantabhadra.
Avalokiteshvara is a serene smile.
She's so nice, but really wise, and just knows the right kind of nice you need.
And Jizo, similar but different, is just about kindness.
He's completely kind to everybody, everybody he sees, and playful, kind and playful, childlike, childlike.
Another thing about all this movement is that it's come through multiple cultures and languages, so the names are really confusing.
Have you noticed that?
There are all these different names for the same thing.
It's been helpful to me to know a little bit about that, so I'll say something about the names.
The Mahayana movement was written down in Sanskrit.

It was probably invented in multiple local languages of these monks in these different monasteries, but it was all written down in Sanskrit, whereas early Buddhism was written down in the South Indian scholastic language of Pali, also not invented in Pali, but written down in Pali.
So we have the Sanskrit name for all these characters: Manjushri, Sanskrit; Avalokiteshvara, Sanskrit; and this week the somewhat difficult to say Kshitigarbha, also Sanskrit.

But then all the East Asian Buddhist schools went through China, just the way the flow went out of Northern India, down the Silk Road into China, and then radiating back outward to Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Mongolia.
And in our case, eventually America.
It just kept going around the world from Japan.
The Chinese figured out Chinese characters that had more or less the same sound as the Sanskrit, so they did a transliteration.
Each of these major bodhisattvas has a two-character Chinese name, so even the ones that sound pretty long in Sanskrit are two words.
Avalokiteshvara, right, Avalokiteshvara, Avalokiteshvara became Guanyin, right, and then became Kanan in Japan.
To make things even more confusing, Kanan is the Japanese voicing of the same character the Chinese picked to transliterate that.
So it's the same name, it just got reformatted moving across cultures.
The Asian languages are so deep and interesting, and especially somehow the Japanese.
Maybe the other Asian cultures are equally multi-layered and wacko, but I know a little bit about Japanese.
Desiree knows a little more than me.

The Japanese borrowed the entire set of Chinese characters, but they weren't hanging around with Japanese speakers, they had their own way of speaking, so they made up their own ways of saying all the characters.
Now they're pronouncing the same exact character in a totally different way.
And then when they started using those characters in everyday language as well, they ended up with two different ways they'd say the same character.
One way, if it was a name or something really Japanese-y, which was very high culture, like high Latin, they had one way.
And then for everyday usage they would have another way, which persists to this day.
Sometimes very similar, almost the same, sometimes a hugely different sound for the same character.
Then it all gets turned into English, and so we have the Romanization of it all, and they look radically different.
But to a Japanese person, you'd be looking at the same character.
And Joan knows a lot about this too, actually, so you all can correct me later on what parts I got mixed up.
I just thought it would be useful to know how Kshitigarbha becomes [unclear: "Dijon"], becomes Jizo.
And then, as Taigen mentioned, there's the pronunciation in Korean, which I've forgotten, but it's the same process, same character.
Jizo is one of the great Bodhisattvas for sure, but in the kind of vast literature, he's not as featured.
And you may have noticed in our liturgy, we feature two of the first guys, Manjushri and Avalokiteshvara.
They're mentioned by name every time we do a service.
We're always thinking about wisdom and compassion.
That's our main gig.
Then in the Buddha halls, often if there's a third Bodhisattva, it's Samantabhadra, and on occasional special ceremonies we mention Samantabhadra.
But we rarely mention Jizo.
In Japan, Jizo is quite a popular figure.
We just bring him up once a year, and we actually took a year off this year, so it's been a while.
We bring him up in our New Year's ceremony, because at the end of the New Year's ceremony we recite the names of all the people we've had on the altar that year.
Some of them we recite, and some of them we actually burn, the little name papers, in a sacred fire.
Jizo's main big job as a Bodhisattva is journeys: journeys in life and journeys in between lives, and particularly journeys of young lives that ended so soon.
So we invoke Jizo Bodhisattva in the New Year's ceremony when we're acknowledging all those who were ill this year, all those who have passed this year.
Then we recite his mantra, which is a great little mantra.
I'll just chant it a couple of times.
It goes like this.
Sorry, let me try it again.
I haven't done it a lot.
*Ka, ka, ka, ka-ba-samaya, sva-ha.
So om, ka, ka, ka-ba-samaya, sva-ha.*
Sva-ha, we've heard.
That's the end of a lot of mantras, including the Heart Sutra mantra.
And om, we all know om, that's om like homage.
I didn't look up the ka and ka, ka-ka and ka-ba-mane.
I'll look it up later.
If you know, you can tell us in a bit.
And Samaya, I believe, refers to samsara, but I didn't check that.
The mantras are partly literal meanings and partly powerful sounds.
There are whole schools of Buddhism that emphasize sacred sounds.
In Japan, the Shingon school does this, lots of chanting and emphasizing the sacred power of sound itself.
Which brings us back to scholasticism.
Our Western orientation is that everything should make sense and have a reason and have a history.
Sure, cool.

But it's also wonderful to have these practice influences that we've been lucky enough to encounter and understand, at least enough to feel into a little bit, to remind us it's not just about meaning and history and origins and what's it about.
It's also a feeling and a power that's evoked by sound, by movement, by presence, by breathing and by being.

So we honor Jizo both by being enthusiastic helpers of all beings, like all the other bodhisattvas are, but also by his image and his sacred mantra, and or her, the gender is pretty much ambiguous in all of them.
They get talked about in one gender or another principally, but all the great bodhisattvas are not exactly gendered in that literal way.
They show up with different genders.
Yeah, we have an early precursor of our current gender fluidity with bodhisattvas, which is wonderful.
Didn't think about that till now.
Everybody's a Buddhist, it seems.

And Jizo is often depicted, I'll show you a few pictures of Jizo, as a really youthful monkish character, usually with a shaved head, which is also gender ambiguous, nuns in Japan also shave their heads, carrying a staff with six rings representing the six realms in Buddhist cosmology.
Jizo is also completely transparent, always relating to everybody, no matter what kind of person they are.
He's completely happy to support you.
Whether you're in a blissful, godly realm, he'll help you out.

Whether you're a jealous ashura, this is great, but it's not enough, whether you're a human with all of our mixed-up foibles but the great opportunity we have to practice and awaken, he'll help us out.

If you're in the animal realm, which in Buddhist cosmology is a little simple, I think it's sort of basic instincts, I would like to re-imagine the animal realm as something a little more in the ecological vein, but that's another story.
And he absolutely is big on dipping into the lowest two of the six realms.
The realm of the hungry ghosts, who are always suffering and never quite satisfied, can't get enough, nothing satisfying in them.
And the hell realms, which in Buddhism are varied and graphic and wild, and aren't exactly a punishment, but more a natural result of unhealthy choices, negative karmic acts of body, speech and mind.
Unlike in the western heavens and hells, they aren't permanent states.
You could be there a really, really long time, but they're not permanent.
So a Jizo can actually reduce your sentence, and can show up there and help you understand your karma so that you don't have to be in hell as long.

Some of the famous stories of Jizo that Taigen mentions from the Jizo Sutra are about that, especially examples where Jizo appeared in the form of a daughter, so the gender fluidity is here, whose mothers have done bad things.
These Jizo daughters are willing to go to hell, and presumably the risk is you're going to get stuck there, too.
It's not a small thing.
And they give their mothers teachings to help their mothers reform, basically come to understanding and not have to be in hell quite as many thousands of eons.
I won't get sidetracked by the hells, but they're wonderfully horrible.
Really great.

So let me show you a few images of Jizo, because the other thing that's really great about Jizo is that even though [unclear: "Hishi"] is not a huge figure in the Buddhist literature, there's one principal long Sutra.
I don't know how often Jizo is mentioned otherwise, or Kshitigarbha, [unclear: "Boisapa"].
But he's hugely popular in Japan, and we're a Japanese-derived lineage, so we can feel extra fondness for Jizo, because people in Japan are super into Jizo.
You go around in Japan, and let's see if I can find the right page here.
One second.
There we go.

Good.

They get called phallic rocks.
I don't know if we need to use that term or not though, because of what else it connotates.
These are little Jizo stones that don't exactly have faces, that have little bibs on them.
Just along the side of the road there you can see it's a street with a car behind it.
So all over the place in Japan there are these little shrines to Jizo, either Jizo in this really simple stone form, and each of these little [unclear: "rub"] has four characters on it.
You can see the character for Buddhism on there, but I didn't try to look up what they are.
But then more often little sweet little figures like these guys, and they're given clothing, and oftentimes each of the little Jizo babies represents a child who has passed.
So maybe the clothing was made by the parent of the child, or by a priest, or by somebody, whether it's a reference.
Yeah, just along the side of the road here again.
Here you can see little faces, little Jizos with their bibs.
Maybe the bibs represent rakusu too, I'm not sure.
They're often in lines by temples.
Oops, what happened to this one?
Oh, there we go.
Sometimes they're very worn.

Several temples that I got to visit in Japan had lines of Jizos like this.

Another great reason to really think about Jizo is that one of our great Zen neighbors to the south, Great Vow Monastery of the Zen community of Oregon, is in a little coastal town of Klatskany, an hour and a half from Portland.
The name of the monastery, Great Vow, is a reference to Jizo.
It refers to Jizo's Great Vow to save all beings in all realms, continually helping them.
One of the two founder teachers there, Jozen [unclear: "Beisro"], wrote a wonderful little book about Jizo.

As a little sidebar note about how this is all just about offerings, it's always just about offerings: it turns out Jozen Roshi took a monetary advance when she got the contract to write that book, but the book sold so modestly that she's still paying back the advance.
So this isn't about profit, that's for sure.
It's about offerings to others, whether you're an author or a sculptor or a practitioner or whatever you are.
And here's how Jizo is sometimes depicted, in this very simple line drawing.
He's one of the few Bodhisattvas or Buddhas that's often depicted standing, because he's a journeyer.
He's always traveling around.
He doesn't have time to sit around; he's always going between realms helping beings.

Other Bodhisattvas are usually depicted seated: Manjushri in a lotus meditation posture, Guanyin sometimes that way, sometimes with one knee up in the pose of royal ease, kind of more open and serene that way, somehow more accessible.
Samantabhadra is often riding an elephant because he's got work to do.
Jizo's walking.
And the staff has six little rings that ring when you walk, to warn beings that you're coming, to let them know, good news or bad news, depending on how you look at it.

The last thing I want to share on the screen with you is that when they refer to these sutras in these texts, so Taigen's referring to the Earth Store Bodhisattva Sutra, in the internet age you can often just Google it and find the actual sutra.
Here it is.

I'm basically a little lazy.
I need structure, which actually occurred to me this morning.
I always felt apologetic about that, but I don't have to feel apologetic.
It's okay to need structure.
So I recommend it.
Get yourself in some position where you have to show up.

I just want to share a little bit of the sutra and say a few more things about Jizo, not too many, and then open up our discussion.

I'll read the first couple of paragraphs and skip a little, and a little bit more and skip a little, and a little bit more, so you just get a sense of what this source text is like.
It's similar to all the other Mahayana sutras, and those of us studying the Diamond Sutra will notice some similarities too.
*Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was in the [unclear: "Trata Sramaya"] heaven, so heavens, speaking dharma for his mother.

At that time, uncountably many Buddhas and great Bodhisattva Mahasattvas from infinite worlds in the ten directions assembled to praise how Shakyamuni Buddha is able to manifest powerfully great wisdom and spiritual penetrations in the evil world of the five turbidities.
They lauded how he regulates and subdues obstinate beings so they can learn what causes suffering and what brings bliss.
Each sent his attendants to pay their respects to the world-honored one.
At that time, the world-honored one smiled, emitted billions of great light clouds.

There was a light cloud of great fullness, a light cloud of great compassion, a light cloud of great wisdom, a light cloud of great prajna, a light cloud of great samadhi, a light cloud of great auspiciousness, a light cloud of great blessings, a light cloud of great merit, a light cloud great refuge and a light cloud of great praise.*
*And after emitting indescribably many light clouds, he also uttered many wonderfully subtle sounds.
There was the sound of Dhanaparamita, the sound of Shilaparamita, the sound of Kshantiparamita, the sound of Viryaparamita, Dhyanaparamita, and the sound of Prajnaparamita.

There was the sound of great compassion, the sound of joyous giving, the sound of liberation, the sound of no outflows, the sound of wisdom, the sound of great wisdom, the sound of the lion's roar, the sound of the great lion's roar, the sound of thunder clouds, the sound of great thunder clouds.*
It goes on like that for quite a long time, all the miraculous things the Buddha does.
You thought he just gave really elegant teachings.
That would have been the early Buddhism.
This is very characteristic of the Mahayana.
It's like, not only did they imagine gender fluidity thousands of years ago, they also imagined science fiction thousands of years ago.
Then it goes on quite a while to list all the bodhisattvas who showed up.
At first they just sent their emissaries, as it said, but then it was so cool they all became a person.
So this huge vast assembly of bodhisattvas is here, and it lists them all off as it does.
Then Manjushri is there.
So remember your first bodhisattva of the series, the wisdom bodhisattva.
He's so blown away by the Buddha, and has been for a long time, ever since he realized the truth.

He says to the Buddha, and it's a pretty common way to get a sutra going, it's very similar in the Lotus Sutra and many other sutras: oh, I am so delighted, as are all these gazillion bodhisattvas, in your wondrous teachings, and I understand them deeply.
But I'm a little worried, dear Buddha.
There may be those who don't really understand or don't accept it.
Sometimes they do insert a little dig against the early Buddhists in that section.
This is human cultural stuff as well as wisdom text.
And they say, yeah, those early guys might not get it, so we have to help them out.
The Buddha, towards the end of his intro and all this incredible stuff, had mentioned Jizo.
He just mentioned him, mentioned that Jizo had been there through all this.
So Manjushri humbly requests of the Buddha, would you please tell everybody about Jizo Bodhisattva's great practice, because I think they'll relate to that.
That'll make sense to them and then they'll come around to the truth.
Another great thing to notice about these texts is that it all revolves around teaching and understanding, as it said in that first paragraph.
That's really worth noticing.
The Buddha didn't magically straighten people out.
The root idea of all the teachings was always what it said there: what leads to suffering, what leads to liberation, helping people to understand that.
But they have to understand for themselves.
So first the Buddha explains how much great stuff Jizo has done.
He uses a metaphor which may sound very familiar to you from the Diamond Sutra.
The Buddha says to Manjushri, oh, it's good you brought up Jizo again.
Let me tell you how much Jizo has done for us here.
Think about this.
Take every blade of grass and shoot of bamboo and lots of other plants and think of each one as an entire Ganges River.
The number of incredible beings in the vast assembly who've been helped by Jizo is as vast as the number of grains of sand in every one of those Ganges Rivers.
They're always taking it another level up.
They also invented exponential progressions.

And every one of those beings, as many as the grains of sand, and there are as many rivers as there are blades of grass, blah, blah, blah, has been helped across to the other shore by Jizo, by Earth Store Bodhisattva.
Manjushri says that's really wonderful.
Please, please tell them how he did it.
How did he practice?
And then the bulk of the rest of the sutra, as Taigen mentioned, is a series of stories about Jizo, all organized around and explained as Jizo in past lives and past forms.
I'll just share one of them with you.
What's great and overwhelming about these kinds of materials is that you could spend many years on any one of these texts.
So he says to Manjushri, well, Manjushri, indescribably many eons ago, during the time of an earlier Buddha, that Buddha was called Lion Sprint Complete.
So, a Buddha like a lion sprinting, Lion Sprint Complete, and there would have been a Sanskrit name that's translated.
At that time, Jizo was the son of a great elder.
This elder son was really Jizo.

Upon observing the Buddha of that age's hallmarks and fine features, and seeing the thousand blessings of that, he asked that Buddha what practices and vows led to him looking like that, led to him expressing that radiant enlightenment.
And so the Buddha of that age, Lion Sprint Complete, also, actually, here's the full name, it's so fun, his full name was Lion Sprint Complete in the 10,000 practices thus come one.
He said to the elder son:
*If you wish to have a body like mine, you must first spend a long time liberating beings who are undergoing suffering.*
That's how you do it.
That's the practice.
Spend a really long time liberating beings who are undergoing suffering.
That comment caused the elder son, this prior Jizo, to make a great vow.
*From now until the ends of future time, through uncountable eons, I will use expansive expedient devices to help beings in all of the six paths who are suffering for their offenses.
Only when they have all been liberated will I myself become a Buddha.*
*From the time you made that great vow in the presence of that Buddha until now, hundreds and thousands of nayutas of inexpressibly many eons have passed, and he is still a Bodhisattva.*
So the point being he didn't pop over into Buddhahood, but he's cheerfully a Bodhisattva.
So that's the great vow.
And Jizo, I suppose, is also the patron saint of reform.
No matter how messed up you are, he believes in you, believes that you can redeem yourself.
So he goes to prison, hells, and all kinds too.
After telling many, many, many stories like this, which I didn't read them all, I scammed a bit, it ends with the 26 benefits to us now of benefiting Jizo.
I won't read you all 26, it takes a little while, but I'll read a selection of them and you can look it up.
If you really appreciate Jizo in your practice, you will be protected by gods and dragons.
You won't retreat from Bodhi.
So if you start to feel some enlightenment, you won't freak out, you won't retreat.
That's good.
It's also really good for right now because you will not be infected by epidemics.
Good.
You won't be threatened by thieves and lots of other disasters.
You'll be protected from them.
You'll be upright and have a proper appearance, if they care about appearance.
Your family will be happy.
You will always arrive at your destination, so he's a Bodhisattva of travelers.
Your dreams will be peaceful and happy.
Your deceased relatives will leave suffering behind.
That's a really important part of Jizo's practice: helping deceased relatives who are suffering.
They'll know peace, and you'll be intelligent and have keen faculties and be magnanimous and empathetic.
And ultimately, the last benefit, ultimately, twenty-eight benefits actually, ultimately you will realize Buddhahood.
So that's good, huh?
But in the interest of not whitewashing anything, there are two unfortunate benefits.
Buddhism was not exempt from misogyny, so I just want to mention this for full disclosure.
One of the benefits in this ancient text of venerating Buddha is that if you're a woman, you can be reborn as a man.
Similarly, you can also be born as the daughter of a national leader or official who presumably is male.
So good to know these things are always a mix: beautiful, wondrous and culturally conditioned, in a mess just like us.
So it's great to appreciate Jizo, and we had a little Jizo garden at Forest Street.
We started one.
It's something I always meant to work on some more.
We'll try again once we have another plot of ground.

And a couple of times we did a wonderful contemporary ceremony adapted from Japanese Buddhism, inviting people to come and sew those little red bibs and put them on our little Jizos, or your own Jizo at home, as a way of honoring those in your lives who have passed, especially those who passed as fetuses or babies, for whatever reason.
It was so beautiful.
I got to do it a couple of times.
Andrea Thatch, when she was up, had learned the ceremony from leaders in the Bay Area, and so she shared it with us.
So we have that from Andrea.
Thank you, Andrea.
I was very moved one of the times.
Somebody I had been practicing with for many years came and shared with us about suffering she was holding from an abortion early in life.
It was so moving that she could invite Jizo Bodhisattva with us to help release a little more of the suffering that was there.
She told us a little bit about what had happened.
So it goes deep, this work of Jizo.
I always enjoy being cheerful about talking about this stuff, but it's also about the deep suffering of the world.
There's suffering in all the six realms.
You could think about them cosmologically as being reborn in this state or that state, and that may be true.
What do we know?
But Taigen also talks about this nicely in the book.
